case.presentation: A 78-year-old woman with history of hyperlipidemia, androgenetic alopecia, TIA, and osteopenia (on alendronate for the past year) presents because her dentist plans a tooth extraction with bone graft and implant. She is at high fracture risk due to her advanced age and weight, but no other FRAX risk factors. She is concerned about medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ). Her only other medications are aspirin and atorvastatin. When should alendronate be held and resumed with respect to the procedure?
case.recommendations: MRONJ is extremely rare in patients receiving alendronate for osteoporosis (estimated 1/10,000–1/100,000). While invasive jaw surgery such as extraction with graft may impart a slightly higher risk, especially if periodontal disease or other risk factors (diabetes, smoking, steroids) coexist, routine dental procedures and implants do not significantly increase MRONJ incidence. In a high-fracture-risk patient, the fracture-prevention benefit of bisphosphonates far outweighs the low MRONJ risk. Therefore, do not interrupt it for the dental procedure. Emphasize optimal dental hygiene; the dentist may use perioperative oral antibiotics and antimicrobial rinses or local antimicrobials as appropriate.

options.text: Inform patient that alendronate is absolutely contraindicated in any dental procedure and must be stopped permanently
Inform patient that dental implants are contraindicated while on bisphosphonates
Reassure patient that MRONJ only happens with IV bisphosphonates for cancer and the risk is zero with oral pills
Warn patient about signs of MRONJ to report (exposed bone, pain, swelling, infection)
Order bone density scan (DEXA)
